Beállítom Kiskunfélegyháza külterületén, Felsőgalamboson ütött ki a sokadik bozót- és erdőtűz az országban csütörtökön, de ez volt az első, ami halálos áldozatot is szedett. A Baon.hu vármegyei portál szerint öthektárnyi terület kapott lángra a 6. dűlőtől nyugatra. Csányi József polgármester egy helyszíni videóban elmondta, egy tanya mellett keletkezett a tűz, majd az épületre is átterjedt, ami leégett. Az ingatlan 84 éves tulajdonosa életét vesztette a tűzben. A helyszínen nagy erőkkel dolgoztak a tűzoltók, a munkájukat a környéken élők és gazdák is segítették. A lap szerint sokan traktorokkal, lapátokkal és locsolókocsikkal érkeztek, így sikerült megfékezni a lángokat. A polgármester azt kérte a lakosságtól, kerülje el az érintett területet, valamint segítse a tűzoltók közlekedését. A Baon hozzátette, csütörtökön ez már a második tűzeset volt Kiskunfélegyháza környékén. Délelőtt egy tanyaépület és több hektár tarló gyulladt ki az M5-ös autópálya közelében. A lángok egy fás területet és vasúti talpfákat is érintettek, a tüzet több település egységei fékezték meg a cikk szerint. Később a Szabóhegyi dűlőn is felcsaptak a lángok a bozótban, ezek egy melléképületre is átterjedtek. Itt a kecskeméti hivatásos és a lajosmizsei önkormányzati tűzoltók avatkoztak be. A nap folyamán komoly tűz keletkezett Jánoshalma és Kunfehértó között is, itt a fenyves kapott lángra nagyjából 6 hektáron. A kiskunhalasi, kiskőrösi hivatásos és a jánoshalmai önkormányzati tűzoltók hat vízsugárral oltották el végül bajai, kalocsai és paksi vízszállítók segítségével. https://www.dw.com/en/sweden-several-wou.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5JD8f Police locked down other schools in the area following the attack Image: Niklas Hagman/TT/picture alliance Advertisement A person armed with a sword has wounded multiple people at a school in Fagersta in central Sweden , authorities said Friday. Police said one person had been taken into custody and there was no longer any danger to the public. "Two people are seriously wounded," Jonas Cederberg, healthcare director in Vastmanland county in central Sweden, told reporters. Swedish media reported that the perpetrator is a man and that police shot him in the leg. That information has not been independently verified. What else do we know? Police were called to the Brinellskola, a secondary school in Fagersta, at around 2 p.m. local time (1200 GMT). The school, which has some 450 students aged 16 to 20, had just reopened after the summer holidays. Public broadcaster SVT reported that ambulances, police cars and a police helicopter were outside the property. The municipality said other schools and some public buildings in the area had been locked down. Fagersta, home to some 12,000 people, lies around 170 kilometers (105 miles) northwest of the capital, Stockholm. Reactions to 'terrible news' "Our thoughts are with all those affected," Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson said in a post on X. "We do not yet know what lies behind the act, but we know that the police are working very intensively." Magdalena Andersson, leader of the opposition Social Democrats, lamented the "terrible news." "When violence takes place at a school, I know it impacts everyone in our country. All of Sweden ⁠stands together with Fagersta at this difficult time," she wrote on X. Other attacks at educational institutions Sweden has seen a number of high-profile attacks at educational facilities in recent years. In February 2025, a 35-year-old man killed 10 people at an adult education center in Orebro. In another incident, an 18-year-old student fatally stabbed two teachers at a Malmo high school in March 2022. Don't let the algorithm hide the news. Photograph: CDC/Reuters North Carolina North Carolina teenager dies from rare infection caused by brain-eating amoeba Naegleria fowleri is commonly found in warm freshwater, and if it enters through the nose, can cause brain damage Maya Yang Mon 31 Aug 2026 17.34 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A North Carolina teenager has died after contracting a rare and often fatal brain-eating amoeba. The state’s health department (NCDHHS) confirmed the boy’s death on Monday, saying: “NCDHHS has been informed that the teen who developed a rare illness, caused by Naegleria fowleri died on Aug. 31, 2026. We extend our condolences to the family, friends and community impacted by this loss.” Last Thursday, NCDHHS reported that the boy had contracted a rare illness caused by the single cell organism commonly found in warm freshwater. The teenager – whose mother, Monica Mendoza, identified him as Moises Ponce Mendoza in an online fundraiser – was described earlier by the NCDHHS in its statement as “critically ill and receiving medical care”. A Facebook post from a user who identified himself as a close relative of Ponce – also said that the teen had died by Monday. Devastation, doubt and blame: Hurricane Helene looms over North Carolina’s US Senate race Read more In the online fundraiser, Mendoza described her son in Spanish as a “young man full of life currently fighting for his life in the hospital – in a coma”, adding that his illness started with severe headaches. She said she initially took Moises to a Burlington hospital for severe symptoms on 21 August – but they were sent home after a doctor briefly examined him. His condition quickly worsened and Mendoza said she rushed him to the University of North Carolina hospital’s emergency department at 7am the next day. Doctors there found he had an infection caused by Naegleria fowleri, which she described as “an extremely rare amoeba that can enter through the nose, reach the brain, and cause inflammation, infection, and brain damage”. “From that moment on, our lives changed completely,” Mendoza added. “Moises is in a coma, and doctors are doing everything possible to fight this illness and give him a chance to pull through.” Pictures posted online showed Moises intubated in a hospital bed and receiving intravenous fluids. The Guardian has contacted Mendoza for additional comment. Naegleria fowleri is often found in warm ponds, lakes and rivers. It is not found in saltwater or in properly maintained and chlorinated pools, the NCDHHS said. The amoeba is harmless if swallowed – but is often deadly if contaminated water enters the nose and reaches the brain, such as while diving in water, water-skiing or engaging in similar activities. Naegleria fowleri can cause an infection known as primary amebic meningoencephalitis (PAM), according to the US Centers of Disease Control (CDC). Its symptoms can include severe headaches, fever, nausea and vomiting, followed by stiff neck, seizures and coma, with the illness often progressing rapidly and causing death within about five days. Fewer than 10 cases are typically reported in the US each year, usually during prolonged periods of hot weather when freshwater temperatures rise, the NCDHHS warned. The CDC says more than 97% of people who contract PAM die from the infection. Health officials advise swimmers to keep their heads above water in warm freshwater, use nose clips or hold their noses shut when entering the water, and avoid diving or jumping in. They also recommend avoiding submerging the head in hot springs or thermal waters and disturbing sediment in shallow, warm freshwater. Ponce’s story gained attention after an eight-year-old Louisiana girl died after contracting a Naegleria fowleri infection. Lillian Smart may have been infected while she was swimming in Louisiana’s Lake Claiborne, the Louisiana health department said. The girl died on 23 August, eight days after she was hospitalized. As the climate crisis continues to alter environmental conditions, scientists warn that Naegleria fowleri is being detected in parts of the US where it has not traditionally been found, with the amoeba appearing to expand from southern states into the Midwest. “It likes warm surface waters during the summer in the northern latitudes,” Charles Gerba, a University of Arizona microbiologist, told the Guardian in 2022. Photograph: Andrés Martínez Casares/Reuters View image in fullscreen Haiti's president Jovenel Moïse speaks during a press conference in March 2020. Photograph: Andrés Martínez Casares/Reuters Haiti More than a dozen arrested in connection with 2021 assassination of Haitian president Jovenel Moïse, 53, was shot dead in July 2021 in a killing which sparked chaos in Haiti Agence France-Presse Sun 20 Sep 2026 16.17 EDT Last modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 17.24 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Eighteen people have been arrested in association with the 2021 assassination of the Haitian president Jovenel Moïse, according to US officials. Moïse, 53, was shot dead on 7 July 2021 at his private residence by a hired group of about 20 military-trained Colombian mercenaries. His security detail did not intervene to protect him. “Today’s multi-location and international arrests underscore the FBI’s continued commitment to bringing all participants in this plot to justice,” FBI special agent Brett Skiles said on Sunday. The suspects have been taken to Florida to stand trial. In the same post on X, federal prosecutor Jason Reding Quinones said: “18 transported in military plane from Haiti to face American justice in the southern district of Florida.” “Five years later, we are still bringing defendants before American courts, and we are not finished,” Quinones wrote, adding that 30 suspects have thus far been indicted in the killing. In May, four men were convicted in a federal court in Miami of charges including conspiracy to kill or kidnap Moïse, conspiracy to provide material support and violating the US Neutrality Act to engage in an illicit military operation abroad. The men face possible sentences of life in prison. All four were linked to CTU, a private security firm based in Florida, and lured into the plot by the prospect of securing lucrative contracts in the event of Moïse’s ouster, according to federal prosecutors. Eleven people have already been indicted in connection with the assassination in US courts, which have jurisdiction over plots hatched on American soil. Five of them have been sentenced to life in prison, including a former Colombian soldier, a former Haitian senator, a Haitian Chilean businessman, a retired Colombian soldier and a Haitian American. Haiti has descended into deeper chaos since Moïse’s killing, and currently has no president. It is preparing to hold its first presidential and legislative election since 2016, as well as a referendum on the constitution, on 13 December – if security conditions allow. Gangs control about 80% of Port-au-Prince, and violent crimes such as kidnappings for ransom, armed robbery and carjackings plague the impoverished nation. A UN-backed armed force tasked with helping local police combat gangs will not be fully staffed by October as planned, its spokesperson said earlier this month. Announced by the UN security council last year, the Gang Suppression Force was expected to ramp up between April and October to a planned capacity of 5,500 uniformed personnel and 50 civilian staff. As of July, it comprised fewer than 1,000 personnel from Chad, Mongolia, Jamaica, Guatemala, El Salvador and Sri Lanka. More recent figures have not been disclosed. https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: Official data released at 11:30am are expected to show inflation accelerated to 4.2% in the year to September, from 4% in the month before, as rising fuel costs amid a worsening Middle East conflict compound cost of living pressures. Look out for the Reserve Bank’s preferred gauge of underlying inflation, which removes the most volatile prices. That measure is predicted to hold at 3.6% in the year to the September quarter, economists say, but anything higher will virtually guarantee a fifth interest rate hike next Tuesday. The RBA may feel the need to hike regardless, as recent comments from top central bank officials suggest they are more worried about high inflation becoming entrenched in the system than the rising rate of unemployment. Financial markets are pricing in about a 65% chance of a Melbourne Cup day rate rise.
